title: Grammar: 'Hay' vs. 'Está'
description: Master the difference between 'hay' (there is/are) and 'está' (is located).

sentences.spanish: Hay un libro en la mesa.
sentences.english: There is a book on the table.

sentences.spanish: En mi calle hay una panadería muy buena.
sentences.english: On my street there's a very good bakery.

sentences.spanish: No hay leche en la nevera.
sentences.english: There's no milk in the fridge.

sentences.spanish: ¿Hay un supermercado por aquí?
sentences.english: Is there a supermarket around here?

sentences.spanish: Sí, hay uno en la esquina.
sentences.english: Yes, there's one on the corner.

sentences.spanish: En Madrid hay muchos museos.
sentences.english: In Madrid there are lots of museums.

sentences.spanish: Hay un problema con el ordenador.
sentences.english: There's a problem with the computer.

sentences.spanish: ¿Cuántos estudiantes hay en clase?
sentences.english: How many students are there in class?

sentences.spanish: En mi pueblo solo hay dos bares.
sentences.english: In my village there are only two bars.

sentences.spanish: Antes no había tantas tiendas por aquí.
sentences.english: There didn't use to be so many shops around here.

sentences.spanish: Ayer había mucha gente en la plaza.
sentences.english: Yesterday there were lots of people in the square.

sentences.spanish: Hay que madrugar mañana.
sentences.english: We have to get up early tomorrow.

sentences.spanish: El libro está en la mesa.
sentences.english: The book is on the table.

sentences.spanish: La nevera está vacía.
sentences.english: The fridge is empty.

sentences.spanish: Mi coche está en el garaje.
sentences.english: My car is in the garage.

sentences.spanish: ¿Dónde está el baño?
sentences.english: Where is the bathroom?

sentences.spanish: Está al final del pasillo.
sentences.english: It's at the end of the corridor.

sentences.spanish: Las llaves están en el cajón.
sentences.english: The keys are in the drawer.

sentences.spanish: Mis padres están de vacaciones.
sentences.english: My parents are on holiday.

sentences.spanish: El supermercado está cerrado hoy.
sentences.english: The supermarket is closed today.

sentences.spanish: ¿Hay pan?
sentences.english: Is there any bread?

sentences.spanish: El pan está en la bolsa.
sentences.english: The bread is in the bag.

sentences.spanish: Hay una carta para ti.
sentences.english: There's a letter for you.

sentences.spanish: La carta está sobre la mesa.
sentences.english: The letter is on top of the table.

sentences.spanish: En esta zona hay mucho tráfico.
sentences.english: There's a lot of traffic in this area.

sentences.spanish: En mi barrio hay un parque y siempre está lleno de niños.
sentences.english: In my neighbourhood there's a park, and it's always full of children.

grammarExplanation:
'Hay' (from 'haber') expresses the EXISTENCE of something indefinite: Hay un problema = There is a problem. It has only one form for singular and plural. Use it when the thing isn't specific or known yet. 'Estar' tells you WHERE a specific thing or person is: El libro está en la mesa = The book is on the table (we know which book). A good trick: if you can name or point at it, it's probably 'está'. Also learn these two extras:

• Había = there was / there were (past existence)
• Hay que + infinitive = one has to do something (obligation): Hay que madrugar.

Conjugation of estar for location:
• Está = he/she/it is • Están = they are

hay.mnemonic: 'Eye' — with your eye you spot what exists.
hay.explanation: Impersonal form of haber: there is / there are.

había.explanation: Past (imperfect) of hay: there was / there were.

nevera.mnemonic: Never a warm drink in the nevera.

cajón.mnemonic: A cajón is a big box you draw open.

esquina.mnemonic: Around the esquina, the corner shop.

tráfico.mnemonic: Traffic jam on the way to traffic-oh.
